title: GPU memory spike/train analysis — CUDA allocator patterns and workspace sizing
content:
ABSTRACT:
Quick working notes on a recurring class of GPU OOM/spike incidents observed in the hosted inference fleet. Symptoms point at allocator fragmentation and repeated cudaMalloc/cudaFree patterns in the runtime workspace layer, aggravated by mixed-size KV cache allocations during long conversations. This doc captures evidence, repro steps, hypotheses, and short-term mitigations to try in the next dogfood run.

Background / Why this matters:
- Production serving needs predictable tail latency and stable memory usage. We observed intermittent OOMs on p4d and A100 nodes even though aggregate memory usage (per-process high-water mark) stays under instance capacity.
- Root cause appears to be fragmentation and transient peak working set growth during batched requests + cache population. These are especially visible when sequence length or prompt prefixes vary a lot between requests.

Observed symptoms (field notes):
- Sudden cudaErrorMemoryAllocation exceptions from the runtime when handling a burst of 10-20 concurrent requests with variable seq lengths.
- nvidia-smi shows free memory dropping in small steps, then a sudden failure despite there being >10% free reported minutes earlier.
- Process-level high-water mark (RSS-like on GPU) often lower than the largest allocation requested at failure time.
- Logs contain many small cudaMalloc/cudaFree calls during inference hot path (workspace manager doing per-layer allocations for variable attention cache combos).

Quick trace excerpts (sanitized):
- runtime: allocate_workspace(2488320) -> cudaMalloc ptr 0x7f1a1b400000
- runtime: allocate_workspace(327680) -> cudaMalloc ptr 0x7f1a1b7a0000
- ... repeated small allocations/free cycles between transformer layers
- runtime: allocate_workspace(10485760) -> cudaMalloc returned cudaErrorMemoryAllocation at seqLen=2048

Profiling and tools used:
- nvprof / Nsight Systems (lightweight timeline captures). Use --trace=cudaMalloc,cudaFree,memcpy to see allocation churn.
- custom heap-tracker in runtime (REDWOOD_ALLOC_DEBUG=1) that logs allocation sizes, free sizes, and timestamps.
- nsight-sys timeline capture to correlate allocation spikes with host-side request bursts.
- nvidia-smi dmon (1s) for coarse free memory shape.
- RMM metrics when running with pooled allocator (we have a build that can switch runtime allocators).

Repro recipe (dev box / minimal):
1) Launch a single-process serving instance with the same runtime build used in fleet (not a debug-only build).
2) Set environment: EXPORT REDWOOD_ALLOC_LOG=1; export REDWOOD_ALLOC_POOL=off (force system cudaMalloc/free).
3) Start a bench script: bench/spike-concurrency.py with concurrency=16, prompt-lengths sampled from [128,512,2048], burst pattern: 12 reqs over 2s, then 30s idle.
4) Capture nsight sys timeline and REDWOOD_ALLOC_LOG.
Expected: after ~3-6 bursts either OOM or significant allocator churn and high tail latency.

Data collected (high level):
- Allocation histogram shows two clusters: many small allocs in [8KB..512KB] and occasional large ones 8MB..20MB for workspace/residual buffers.
- Free-list fragmentation: largest free chunk metric often < required large allocation although total free memory > needed.
- Enabling a pooled allocator (RMM-style) converted the many small allocations into internal sub-allocations and removed immediate OOMs in the repro; however, pool growth still occasionally hit total GPU memory when long sequences appear concurrently.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Variable per-request workspace sizing + per-layer cudaMalloc/cudaFree leads to fragmentation: small chunks fill the heap, large contiguous allocation fails.
2) Interaction with allocator alignment rules (64k/256k alignment boundaries) causes internal wasted memory and inability to satisfy large contiguous requests even if aggregate free >= request size.
3) KV cache growth + sparse eviction results in many long-lived medium allocations alongside short-lived ones, increasing fragmentation.
4) Default driver/allocator behavior differs across CUDA versions and can exacerbate fragmentation (observed differences between CUDA 11.7 vs 12.x in test fleet).

Short-term mitigations to try (fast experiments):
- Enable pooled allocator with upfront reservation: reserve N% of GPU memory at process start (configurable, e.g., 65%) and carve off a single large contiguous workspace region that the runtime sub-allocates from.
- Normalize workspace requests: round up workspace requests to a set of size buckets (e.g., power-of-two or 256k-aligned buckets) to reduce free-list fragmentation.
- Limit concurrency for high seq-length models at routing layer (temporary rate-limiter per-model/seqLen).
- Pre-allocate and pin largest expected KV cache per-connection on first use, then use sub-allocations; avoid frequent free/alloc cycles for cache buffers.
- As a last-resort, implement best-effort fallback to smaller model variant or shorter seqLen when allocation fails (graceful degrade).

Longer-term work / experiments:
- Implement a lightweight fragmentation metric: maintain largest_free_chunk / total_free ratio and surface in Console. Alert when ratio < 0.25 for > 2 minutes.
- Investigate use of CUDA driver-level virtual memory APIs (cuMemAddressReserve/cuMemCreate) to manage contiguous address spaces for large buffers.
- Add allocator stress tests to CI: randomized allocation/free patterns that mirror our request distributions (seqLen, batch, KV presence) and assert fragmentation thresholds.
- Evaluate whether using CUDA 12.x pool APIs or third-party allocators (RMM, tcmalloc-like GPU allocators) reduces real-world fragmentation.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How much headroom can we safely reserve for pooled allocator without harming multi-tenant density? Need experiments across instance types.
- Is fragmentation worse on older drivers? Run driver-swapped tests across fleet images.
- Can we compute an optimal bucketization strategy (bucket sizes and counts) from production allocation histograms? Need tooling to sample and propose bucket config.
- Should we block model upgrades that increase peak single-request workspace beyond configured pool? Might be necessary for safety.

Quick action items (owner assignment):
- Rahul: implement repro script in infra/bench and run across cuda11.7 / cuda12 images (due 2026-03-12).
- Maya: prototype a bucketized-workspace allocator in the runtime (experiment flag), measure tail OOMs (due 2026-03-20).
- Ava (me): wire a largest_free_chunk metric and expose in Console debug page + add alert rule (due 2026-03-10).

Notes to self / informal observations:
- I noticed that freeing many small buffers immediately before a big alloc sometimes doesn’t recover because freed fragments are non-contiguous. The allocator's coalescing behavior is critical; if driver doesn't coalesce adjacent free blocks quickly, you'll still fail.
- When we switched to RMM pool in a dogfood run, OOMs mostly disappeared but apparent memory pressure increased because pool reserved space up-front — need to tune reservation to balance density.

Appendix: useful commands
- nsight-sys capture: nsight-sys --capture-range=processes --output=trace.qdrep --trace=cudaMemory -- python bench/spike-concurrency.py
- dump allocations logged by runtime: grep "ALLOC" /var/log/redwood/runtime.log | awk '{print $5}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr
- quick check: python tools/gpu_fragmentation_report.py --pid <pid> --histogram > fragmentation.txt

If we can get a reliable reproducible failure and confirm fragmentation/coalescing behavior, the fix path is straightforward: move to a sub-allocation strategy for workspaces + stabilize KV cache sizing. For now, prioritize pooled allocator + routing-level rate limiting for long sequences.

-- Ava

Unresolved: schedule meeting with TF model owners to discuss model-side workspace reductions (possible fused kernels to lower per-layer temp memory).
